newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria digs in ahead of talks with Commonwealth.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria digs in ahead of talks with Commonwealth.

text.p: Eight Commonwealth ministers will travel to Nigeria this week for talks with its military government on speeding up a process to restore democracy to Africa's most populous country.
But there are no signs that the rulers of the West African nation are ready to yield ground on any issue.

Lagos-based diplomats expect Nigeria to hold tenaciously to its stand that it was wrongly suspended from the Commonwealth last year when it defied pleas for clemency and hanged nine minority rights activists including writer Ken Saro-Wiwa.
"On their home turf they will argue even more forcefully that the suspension should be lifted as a pre-condition for dialogue," one diplomat said.
A government spokesman said Nigeria had prepared well for the meeting in Abuja on Tuesday and Wednesday with the eight-nation Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG).
"Our minds are open but our position remains consistent," he said.
The Abuja meeting should have taken place months ago but it was postponed after Nigeria refused to allow CMAG to meet high profile detainees and opposition groups in the country.
In September, Commonwealth officials visited Abuja to try to pave the way for the CMAG ministers but Nigeria said it could not agree to an inquest from the Commonwealth on the country.
"As far as we are concerned that issue has been settled," the Nigerian spokesman said. "We had a fact-finding mission from the United Nations and no other body supercedes that."
The 53-nation Commonwealth groups Britain and its former colonies.

Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi, a tough talking architect turned politician, will head a formidable Nigerian team which includes some of the nation's best known personalities who are not in government but remain influential with the military government.
CMAG is made up of foreign ministers of Britain, Canada, New Zealand, South Africa, Zimbabwe, Ghana, Jamaica and Malaysia.
The two sides met for the first time in May in London where Nigeria insisted that its suspension was unfair and that until this issue is settled there can be no progress on other matters.
The Commonwealth says military ruler General Sani Abacha's timetable to hand over to an elected president by October 1998 is too long and wants it before next year's Commonwealth summit.
The United Nations on the other hand called for support for the Abacha timetable in order for Nigeria to return to democratic rule.
The government insists the programme is on course and will not be changed because of pressure from abroad.
Abacha seized power in the chaos that followed annulment of a 1993 presidential poll by a previous military government.

Many opposition figures are detained or have fled into exile. CMAG wants to meet detainees such as Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of the annulled poll, who has been held since 1994 when he proclaimed himself president.
It also wants to see former military president Olusegun Obasanjo who was jailed last year with 40 other persons over an alleged plot to topple Abacha.

As they were meeting in May, Nigeria freed half a dozen detainees. The CMAG, which had a month before agreed on a set of sanctions against Nigeria including a ban on sporting links and arms sales, postponed their imposition to allow further talks.
But Nigerian opposition groups, angry that CMAG had succumbed to Abuja, want more action from the group.

"We call on the CMAG to demand, as a conditionality for their visit, the immediate and unconditional release of all political detainees in Nigeria," said the Committee for the Defence of Human Rights (CDHR) pressure group in a statement.
"Unless this is done, the CDHR will have no option than to accuse CMAG of complicity with the Nigerian fascists," it said.
